description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of Bahá'u'lláh's Kalimát-i-Maknúnih, Part I (The Arabic Hidden Words). Contains composition-specific entries: the Hidden-Words-scoped DMG/ALA-LC transliteration and rasm-skeleton conventions; the yā-bna vocative-epithet series (including the insān/bashar distinction); the amr Cause-vs-command split; the mulk/malakūt/jabarūt/ʿamāʾ Sufi-theosophical realm hierarchy; the inṣāf/ʿadl equity-vs-justice distinction; the istishhād fī sabīlī martyrdom idiom; the aḥbār 'the learned' reading; and the Ocean-of-Lights-vs-Bahá'í-World-Centre collation-witness framework with its four retained edition variants. The English is independent of and unaffiliated with the authorised Bahá'í World Centre (Shoghi Effendi) translations. Entries may be promoted to the central production glossary via the standard overlay→central promotion pattern when the lemma acquires cross-corpus reach in subsequent Bahá'í / Bábí / Arabic compositions. NOTE: one proposed entry — the Bahāʾ-root (b-h-y) self-referential onomastic pun — is claim_type=speculative and is NOT included here; it is escalated to the human reviewer in chapter-1-editor-report.md pending explicit sign-off. || PART II EXTENSION (v2.0.0, editor pass 2026-07): adds the Persian-scoped entries required by Part II (The Persian Hidden Words) — the DMG/Encyclopaedia-Iranica Persian transliteration convention; the Persian vocative-epithet series (ای پسر X / ای فرزند X …), which levels the two dust-words khāk (Persian) and turāb (Arabic loan) to 'Dust' as interchangeable synonyms, unlike the Part I insān/bashar distinction; the Persian Sufi bestiary and cosmological toponyms (bulbul, ʿanqā/phoenix, Qáf, hudhud/Sheba, Humá, varqāʾ) with their retain-vs-gloss policy; and the HWP-71 Sinai covenant toponyms (Fārān=Párán, Madyan=Midian, Zamān='Time' not a named locus). Existing entries reused across both Parts (cosmological realm hierarchy; inṣāf/ʿadl; amr — now carrying an explicit third 'affair/matter' register) have had their appliesTo extended to the governed HWP refIds; this is the semver-major change. No new speculative entry is committed: the b-h-y (Bahāʾ) self-referential onomastics — including HWP-77's letter-by-letter naming of the Name (bāʾ+hāʾ) — is kept NEUTRAL in the surface text per the ratified Part I human ruling of 2026-07-03 and is escalated for explicit re-confirmation in chapter-2-editor-report.md.

entries.lemma: the project-specific scientific-transliteration convention for Arabic source-text rendering in the Hidden Words: DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) with ALA-LC (American Library Association / Library of Congress) compatibility; underdot for emphatic consonants (ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ ḥ); ḫ for the kh-sound, ġ for the gh-sound, š for shīn, ḏ for ḏāl, ṯ for thāʾ; ʿ for ʿayn, ʾ for hamza; macron for long vowels (ā ī ū); double consonants for shadda; sun-letters assimilated in the article (aš-šams, an-nūr, ar-rūḥ); the definite article written joined before sun-letters and hyphen-separated otherwise
entries.standardEnglish: DMG / ALA-LC convention as the project standard for Arabic-source-text transliteration
entries.wohChoice: the translit field reflects the DMG / ALA-LC convention, identical in scheme to the Qur'an-WoH convention entry; this entry scopes that convention to the Hidden Words (HW-WOH)
entries.rationale: The Hidden Words are the project's second Arabic-source text after the Qur'an, and the translit field adopts the same DMG (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft) convention with ALA-LC compatibility already established for the Qur'an-WoH translation. The convention is the academic standard in modern Islamic-, Bábí-, and Bahá'í-studies publications (Encyclopaedia of Islam, 3rd ed., Brill; Encyclopaedia Iranica; the Journal of Bahá'í Studies scholarly apparatus), and is distinct both from popular-English digraph transliteration (th/kh/gh/sh) and from the IJMES scheme. This overlay entry exists because the Qur'an-WoH transliteration-convention entry's appliesTo array covers only QUR-WOH refIds; the Hidden Words require their own scoped authorization rather than silently reusing the Qur'an entry. Named references: C. Brockelmann, Geschichte der arabischen Litteratur (Leiden 1937-1949), the foundational DMG reference; W. Wright, A Grammar of the Arabic Language, 3rd ed. (Cambridge 1896-1898); the ALA-LC Romanization Tables (Library of Congress). Promotion candidate: if the same convention is applied across further Bahá'í / Bábí Arabic compositions it should be promoted to the central glossary as a project-wide convention (merging with the Qur'an-WoH convention entry).

entries.lemma: the project-specific rasm-field convention for the Hidden Words: (1) the rasm field is the tashkīl-stripped consonantal skeleton of the modern vocalized ar field — the vowel-marks (fatḥa, kasra, ḍamma, sukūn, shadda, tanwīn) are removed; (2) the ornamental invocation brackets ﴿ … ﴾ around the vocative are removed in the rasm; (3) UNLIKE the Qur'an-WoH rasm-paleographic convention, hamza-seating is NOT collapsed and tāʾ-marbūṭa is NOT reduced to hāʾ — the rasm here is a modern-orthography skeleton, not an early-Hijazi paleographic reconstruction, because the Hidden Words (composed 1857-58, Baghdad) have no early-manuscript paleographic layer comparable to the 7th-century Qur'anic Hijazi witnesses
entries.standardEnglish: the tashkīl-stripped skeleton as the convention for the rasm field of the source-ar-1.json and chapter-1.json layers
entries.wohChoice: the rasm field is a modern-orthography consonantal skeleton (tashkīl removed, invocation brackets removed); hamza-seating and tāʾ-marbūṭa are retained as in the modern ar field, NOT normalized as in the Qur'an paleographic convention
entries.rationale: The Hidden Words require a rasm-field convention distinct from the Qur'an-WoH rasm-paleographic convention. For the Qur'an, the rasm field reconstructs the early-Hijazi 7th-century orthography (no iʿjām, no tashkīl, hamza-collapse, tāʾ-marbūṭa-as-hāʾ), because that text has radiocarbon-dated manuscript witnesses (Tübingen Ma VI 165; Codex Parisino-petropolitanus) whose paleography is itself an object of study. The Hidden Words, by contrast, were composed by Bahá'u'lláh in Baghdad c. 1857-58 CE and are transmitted in modern Arabic orthography; there is no early-Hijazi paleographic layer to reconstruct, so the rasm field here is simply the tashkīl-stripped consonantal skeleton of the modern vocalized text with the ornamental invocation brackets removed — a reading aid and search key, not a paleographic claim. This entry documents that the hamza-seating and tāʾ-marbūṭa are deliberately NOT normalized in this rasm (a difference from the Qur'an convention that the Editor flagged), so downstream consumers do not mistake the Hidden-Words rasm for an early-orthography reconstruction. Promotion candidate: if further modern-composition Arabic texts adopt the same tashkīl-strip-only convention it should be promoted to central alongside a renamed distinction from the paleographic convention.

entries.lemma: the vocative-address formula yā bna X ('O Son of X') / yā abnāʾa X ('O Sons of X') that opens every Hidden Word with a shifting genitive epithet; root of ibn/abnāʾ = b-n-w/b-n-y ('son/child'). Members: ar-rūḥ 'the Spirit' (√r-w-ḥ); al-insān 'the human/Man' (√ʾ-n-s); al-bashar 'mortal humankind' (√b-sh-r); al-wujūd 'Being' (√w-j-d); al-bayān 'Utterance' (√b-y-n); an-nūr 'Light' (√n-w-r); al-manẓar al-aʿlā 'the Supreme Vision/Vista' (√n-ẓ-r); al-ʿamāʾ 'the [primal] Cloud' (√ʿ-m-y/ʿ-m-w); al-ʿarsh 'the Throne' (√ʿ-r-sh); al-jamāl 'Beauty' (√j-m-l); al-huwiyya fi l-ghayb 'the Ipseity/Divine Essence in the unseen' (√h-w, √gh-y-b); man qāma fī malakūti nafsihi 'Him who arose in the kingdom of His own self'
entries.literal: O Son of / O Sons of + [genitive epithet]
entries.standardEnglish: the authorised Bahá'í World Centre (Shoghi Effendi) translation levels ibn al-insān AND ibn al-bashar both to 'O Son of Man', and renders 'O Son of Spirit / Being / Utterance / Light / Glory' etc.
entries.wohChoice: rendered literally and epithet-by-epithet, with the two distinct human-lexemes kept distinct: ibn al-insān = 'O Son of Man'; ibn al-bashar = 'O Son of Mortal Man'; ibn ar-rūḥ = 'O Son of the Spirit'; ibn al-wujūd = 'O Son of Being'; ibn al-bayān = 'O Son of Utterance'; ibn an-nūr = 'O Son of Light'; ibn al-manẓar al-aʿlā = 'O Son of the Supreme Vision'; ibn al-ʿamāʾ = 'O Son of the Cloud'; ibn al-ʿarsh = 'O Son of the Throne'; ibn al-jamāl = 'O Son of Beauty'; abnāʾ al-huwiyya fi l-ghayb = 'O Sons of the Divine Essence in the unseen'; ibn man qāma fī malakūti nafsihi = 'O Son of Him who arose in the kingdom of His own self'; plurals abnāʾ al-insān/ar-rūḥ = 'O Sons of Men / O Sons of the Spirit'
entries.rationale: The vocative series is the structural signature of the Hidden Words, and the load-bearing lexical decision is whether to distinguish al-insān from al-bashar in English. Both mean 'the human being', but the roots carry distinct emphases attested in the classical lexica: al-insān (conventionally derived from uns 'intimacy, sociability', or from nasiya 'to forget') denotes the human as such — the rational, God-knowing, intimate creature; al-bashar (cognate with bashara 'skin, outer surface') foregrounds humanity in its mortal, fleshly, created aspect, exactly the nuance of the Qur'anic self-designation basharun miṯlukum 'a mortal like you' (Sura 18:110; 41:6) already fixed in the corpus at the bashar-mortal-quranic-anthropology central entry. The WoH translation therefore renders ibn al-insān 'O Son of Man' and ibn al-bashar 'O Son of Mortal Man', preserving two distinct lexemes that the authorised translation levels to a single 'O Son of Man' — a divergence that both increases lexical precision and keeps the WoH rendering independent of Shoghi Effendi (project requirement). The remaining epithets are rendered by their literal lexical core (Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon, s.vv.), with the cosmological members (al-ʿamāʾ, and the malakūt of the v70 vocative) cross-referenced to the realm-hierarchy entry and al-jamāl / the b-h-y field noted in commentary. Marked inferred rather than direct because the insān/bashar distinction, while lexically defensible, is not the consensus English rendering. Cross-references: cosmological-realm-hierarchy-mulk-malakut-jabarut-amaa-hidden-words-woh; bashar-mortal-quranic-anthropology-cross-corpus-flesh-and-blood-vs-angelic-messenger-expectation (central).

entries.lemma: amr (Arabic; √ʾ-m-r), a term spanning 'command, bidding, order, decree' and 'affair, matter, business', and — as a Bahá'í / Bábí technical term — al-amr 'the Cause' (the divine religion, dispensation, or revealed order; amr Allāh 'the Cause of God'). Occurs across the Hidden Words in both registers
entries.partOfSpeech: Arabic verbal noun; Bahá'í technical term
entries.literal: command / bidding; matter / affair; (technical) the Cause
entries.standardEnglish: 'commandment' / 'bidding' in imperative contexts; 'Cause' as the fixed Bahá'í technical rendering
entries.wohChoice: rendered contextually: 'Cause' where amr denotes the divine religion/dispensation (jawhar amrī HWA-16; rūḥ al-amr … ʿalā l-amr HWA-34; khuḍūʿ li-amrinā HWA-40; ʿaẓẓim amrī HWA-41; nāṣiran li-amrī HWA-42; maṭliʿ amrī HWA-46; kanāʾiz amrī HWA-65) and 'command / bidding' where it denotes an imperative or decree (hāḏā amrī HWA-29, HWA-30; huwa amrī HWA-51)
entries.rationale: amr is one of the most register-sensitive words in the Hidden Words: the same three consonants carry both the plain imperative sense ('this is My command, act upon it') and the fully technical Bahá'í sense of al-amr, 'the Cause' — the divine religious order, later institutionalised as amr Allāh. The WoH translation splits the term contextually rather than flattening it: the institutional/religion occurrences (magnify My Cause; a helper of My Cause; the essence of My Cause; submission to Our Cause; the coffers of My Cause) take 'Cause', while the bare deictic imperatives (hāḏā amrī 'this is My command'; huwa amrī 'this is My command') take 'command / bidding'. This is a defensible reading of the author's usage — Bahá'u'lláh's later corpus makes al-amr a settled technical term, and the Hidden Words already deploy it in that register — but it is not the only possible division (a maximalist could read 'Cause' throughout, a minimalist 'command/bidding' throughout), which is why it is marked inferred, not direct. The split is documented so the Reviewer can confirm or standardise it; the surface English in every case remains a defensible scholarly rendering. Cross-reference: the Qur'anic technical-term precedent for register-sensitive rendering (e.g. dhikr, muḥdaṯ) in the Qur'an-WoH overlay and central entries. PART II (Persian): a third, general 'affair / matter' register is now documented explicitly, alongside the command/decree and technical-Cause senses. NONE of the Part II occurrences bears the settled 'the Cause' sense: turāb-i amr 'the clay of My command' (HWP-29, creative fiat) and ḥasb al-amr 'according to the [divine] command' (HWP-77) are the command/decree register, while hīch amrī 'any matter' (HWP-43) and al-umūr 'affairs' in the Arabic maxim al-umūru muʿallaqatun bi-asbābihā (HWP-80) are the general 'affair/matter' register. appliesTo extended to the governed HWP refIds.

entries.lemma: the Sufi / theosophical cosmological hierarchy invoked across the Hidden Words: mulk (√m-l-k) the dominion / kingship of the created, material realm; malakūt (√m-l-k) the higher angelic kingdom / world of sovereignty; jabarūt (√j-b-r) the realm of divine omnipotence / invincible power; and al-ʿamāʾ (√ʿ-m-y/ʿ-m-w) the primal Cloud — the undifferentiated mist of pre-creation being (cf. lāhūt, the realm of divinity, not lexicalised in Part I)
entries.standardEnglish: these strata are frequently collapsed in English into interchangeable 'kingdom / realm / dominion'; al-ʿamāʾ is sometimes flattened to 'mist', 'blindness', or 'nonexistence'
entries.wohChoice: a fixed, distinct English mapping: mulk = 'dominion'; malakūt = 'kingdom'; jabarūt = 'realm of omnipotence' (in construct, 'the omnipotent realm of X', e.g. jabarūt al-ʿizza = 'the omnipotent realm of glory'); al-ʿamāʾ = 'the Cloud' (capitalised; barr al-ʿamāʾ = 'the wilderness of the Cloud'). This disambiguates mulk from jabarūt, which the draft had both surfacing as 'dominion'
entries.rationale: The Hidden Words repeatedly deploy the technical stratified cosmology of Sufi theosophy — mulk / malakūt / jabarūt (with lāhūt above and ʿamāʾ as the primal undifferentiated ground) — and English renderings routinely collapse the strata into interchangeable 'kingdom/realm/dominion', erasing a structure the Arabic keeps distinct. The WoH translation fixes a one-to-one mapping: mulk 'dominion' (created kingship, HWA-1, 14, 15, 42), malakūt 'kingdom' (the higher angelic sovereignty, HWA-6, 70), jabarūt 'realm of omnipotence' (divine power, prologue, HWA-6), preserving the ascending hierarchy the terms encode. al-ʿamāʾ is rendered 'the Cloud' after its established mystical sense: the primordial Cloud of the ḥadīth 'where was our Lord before He created creation? — He was in a Cloud (fī ʿamāʾ)' (Tirmidhī, Sunan, Tafsīr; Ibn Māja), elaborated by Ibn ʿArabī as al-ʿamāʾ / nafas al-Raḥmān, the cloud of unconditioned Being from which the cosmos is exhaled — against the flatter 'mist' or the homonym ʿamā 'blindness'. Marked inferred because the fixed mapping and the primal-Cloud reading of ʿamāʾ are scholarly, defensible readings (W. Chittick, The Sufi Path of Knowledge, SUNY 1989; H. Corbin, Alone with the Alone / Creative Imagination in the Ṣūfism of Ibn ʿArabī, Princeton 1969) rather than lexically forced. Cross-references: ya-bna-vocative-epithet-series-hidden-words-woh (the ʿamāʾ and man-qāma-fī-malakūt vocatives).

entries.lemma: two distinct justice-terms in the Hidden Words: inṣāf (√n-ṣ-f, 'to halve, to divide evenly'), 'equity, fairness, fair-dealing, giving each their due, discernment' — named at HWA-2 as aḥabb al-ashyāʾ ʿindī 'the best-beloved of all things in My sight'; and ʿadl (√ʿ-d-l, 'to balance, to make equal/straight'), 'justice, righteous dealing, just balance' — at HWA-28
entries.literal: inṣāf = equity / fair-dividing; ʿadl = justice / balancing
entries.standardEnglish: English 'justice' is often used for both, flattening the pair
entries.rationale: The Hidden Words use two different roots for the justice-field, and rendering both as 'justice' erases a distinction the Arabic marks. inṣāf (from n-ṣ-f, 'half') is the act of giving each party its fair half — equity, fair-dealing, even-handed discernment — and is the term Bahá'u'lláh singles out at HWA-2 as 'the best-beloved of all things in My sight', tied there to independent perception ('see with thine own eyes … know by thine own knowledge'); ʿadl (from ʿ-d-l, 'to balance, straighten') is justice as righteous balance, the term at HWA-28 for one who 'bids men be just yet himself commits iniquity'. The WoH translation renders inṣāf 'equity' and ʿadl 'justice', preserving the lexical pair (Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon, s.vv. n-ṣ-f and ʿ-d-l; the inṣāf/ʿadl distinction is also standard in Islamic legal-ethical vocabulary, where ʿadl is the systemic virtue and inṣāf the interpersonal one). Marked inferred because, while the roots are genuinely distinct, English translators legitimately differ on whether to mark the distinction lexically; the WoH choice makes it visible. The echo of the inṣāf root at HWA-46 (fa-anṣif 'be equitable/just') is noted in commentary but not separately entried. PART II: the inṣāf 'equity' reading also governs the Persian vocative pisar-i inṣāf 'O Son of Equity' at HWP-4 and HWP-77 (appliesTo extended).

entries.lemma: the shahāda / istishhād martyrdom vocabulary (√sh-h-d 'to witness'; Form X 'to seek to bear witness = to seek martyrdom'; passive 'to be martyred') combined with the idiom fī sabīl [Allāh] 'in the path [of God]' (√s-b-l): istashhid fī sabīlī 'seek martyrdom in My path' (HWA-45); tustashhad fī sabīlī 'be martyred in My path' (HWA-46); with the associated blood-witness imagery taḵaḍḍub shaʿrika min damika 'dye thy hair with thy blood' (HWA-47) and al-midād al-aḥmar alladhī sufika fī sabīlī 'the crimson ink shed in My path' (HWA-71)
entries.partOfSpeech: Arabic Form X verb + prepositional idiom (technical religious vocabulary)
entries.literal: to seek to bear witness (= to seek martyrdom) / to be made a witness (= to be martyred), in the path of [God]
entries.standardEnglish: 'martyrdom' / 'be martyred' (literal) vs the softened 'offer up / lay down / sacrifice thy life'
entries.wohChoice: literal: 'seek martyrdom in My path' (HWA-45); 'be martyred in My path' (HWA-46); preserving the fī sabīlī 'in the path [of God]' idiom throughout the martyrdom cluster (HWA-45, 46, 47, 71)
entries.rationale: The martyrdom cluster of the Hidden Words uses the shahāda/istishhād vocabulary in its plain, literal sense, and the WoH translation renders it literally — 'seek martyrdom in My path', 'be martyred in My path' — rather than softening it to a purely spiritual 'offer up thy life'. This is a direct reading: the Form X istashhada is lexically 'to seek martyrdom', tustashhada 'to be martyred', and fī sabīl Allāh 'in the path of God' is the fixed Qur'anic idiom for dying in the divine cause (Sura 2:154 'do not say of those slain fī sabīl Allāh that they are dead'; 3:169). Retaining the literal register preserves the doctrinal weight the text carries — martyrdom is a live category in the Bábí-Bahá'í context of the 1850s (the Báb's execution 1850; the mass Bábí martyrdoms) — while the term's extended spiritual sense (self-sacrifice, dying to self, which the surrounding aphorisms about faná/self-effacement support) is noted in commentary rather than substituted into the surface text. The crimson-ink image at HWA-71 (al-midād al-aḥmar … sufika fī sabīlī) and the blood-and-hair image at HWA-47 are rendered literally within the same field. Cross-reference: the Qur'anic fī-sabīl-Allāh martyrdom idiom.

entries.lemma: al-aḥbār (Arabic; sg. ḥibr / ḥabr, √ḥ-b-r), 'the learned, the doctors of religion, the divines' — in Qur'anic and general Islamicate usage often specifically the learned religious authorities of the People of the Book (rabbis, scholars); at the prologue, faḍlan ʿalā l-aḥbār 'as a favour unto the learned', those to whom the gems of the prophetic revelation are entrusted
entries.literal: the learned ones / the doctors / the divines
entries.standardEnglish: the authorised Bahá'í rendering (Shoghi Effendi) has 'unto the righteous'; other renderings range from generalising 'unto men' to the specific 'unto the divines / the doctors of religion'
entries.wohChoice: 'as a favour unto the learned' — the literal reading of aḥbār as the learned religious authorities, against the generalising 'men'
entries.rationale: In the prologue, the gems of the earlier prophetic revelations are 'clothed in the garment of brevity, as a favour ʿalā l-aḥbār'. aḥbār (sg. ḥibr) lexically denotes the learned — the doctors, divines, religious scholars — and in Qur'anic usage (Sura 5:44, 5:63; 9:31, 9:34) refers specifically to the learned authorities of the People of the Book alongside the rabbāniyyūn (Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon, s.v. ḥ-b-r; the Qur'anic aḥbār = rabbis/scholars). The WoH translation renders 'the learned', preserving the sense that the aphorisms are entrusted to those with the discernment to unfold them, rather than the flattening 'men' or 'loved ones'. Marked inferred (though it leans direct) because the lexical reading is clear but the decision to foreground 'the learned' over a generalising rendering is an interpretive choice about the prologue's addressee. The reading is consistent with the prologue's purpose-clause: that the aḥbār 'may fulfil the covenant of God and render up His trusts within their own souls'.

entries.translit: [OL primary transcription; BWC control; four retained edition variants]
entries.lemma: the collation-witness framework for the Hidden Words WoH source: (OL) the Ocean of Lights fully-vocalized e-text is the primary transcription and working source; (BWC) the Bahá'í World Centre authoritative original-language edition is the control, collated verse-by-verse 2026-07-02. Four benign attested edition variants are RETAINED as given by the vocalized OL witness in the ar field and adopted in the English: (1) HWA-61 kuʾūb (كُؤُب, 'cups', pl.) vs BWC kūb (كوب, sg.); (2) HWA-63 the OL pointing nafaḵta (2nd person) where the sense requires nafaḵtu (1st person) — the ar surface is retained, the English/translit adopt the 1st-person reading; (3) HWA-70 OL omits bi-dhātihi ('by His own essence') present in BWC; (4) HWA-71 OL alqaynāka vs BWC alqaynā ilayka (sense identical)
entries.literal: the OL-primary / BWC-control collation framework and its four retained variants
entries.standardEnglish: the Bahá'í World Centre authoritative original-language edition as reference text
entries.wohChoice: OL retained as the working source (its vocalization is fuller than the largely-unvocalized BWC web edition); the four edition-level variants are retained in the ar field and reflected in the English, each recorded here and in per-verse commentary; orthographic house-style differences (hamza-seating, joined vs spaced wāw, yāʾ/alif-maqṣūra) are not tracked as variants
entries.rationale: The Hidden Words WoH source layers a primary transcription (Ocean of Lights, fully vocalized) against a control (the Bahá'í World Centre authoritative original-language edition), collated verse-by-verse on 2026-07-02. The collation found all 71 Arabic Hidden Words substantively identical to the BWC original, with differences confined to orthographic house-style (hamza-seating, wāw spacing, yāʾ/alif-maqṣūra) plus four benign attested edition variants, which were retained as given by the vocalized OL witness rather than silently normalised to BWC. This entry records those four variants so the English is auditable: (1) HWA-61 plural 'cups' (kuʾūb) follows the retained OL reading over BWC singular kūb; (2) HWA-63 the OL surface pointing nafaḵta (2nd person, 'thou didst breathe') breaks the first-person divine-speaker parallelism with the preceding ašraqtu ('I caused to dawn'), so the English and transliteration adopt the expected nafaḵtu (1st person, 'I breathed'), while the ar field retains the witness's pointing and the emendation is flagged rather than silent; (3) HWA-70 follows OL in omitting bi-dhātihi ('by His own essence'), the fuller BWC vocative reading being noted; (4) HWA-71 alqaynāka vs BWC alqaynā ilayka is sense-neutral and recorded for completeness. This is claim_type direct: it documents an editorial/collation fact, not an interpretive reading. Named reference: the Bahá'í Reference Library authoritative original-language edition (bahai.org); the Ocean of Lights e-text (oceanoflights.org). Project policy (strategy-library-acquisition.md) requires verification against pre-1930 lithographs before final sign-off; that verification is pending and is flagged in the editor report. PART II collation (2026-07-02): all 82 Persian Hidden Words were collated OL-vs-BWC and found substantively identical, with NO substantive variants — differences are orthographic house-style only (ezāfe written ۀ/ٔ vs plain ه; attached copula ...ست vs ... است; ترا/تو را; شنیده‌یی/شنیده‌ای). One STRUCTURAL realignment was made to match BWC/authoritative numbering: verse 1's canonical opening clause 'ای صاحبان هوش و گوش، اوّل سروش دوست اینست' had been demoted into the prologue and was moved back verbatim into HWP-1 (no text introduced); the prologue now carries only the invocation heading. No Part II variant is carried in the English.

entries.lemma: the project-specific scientific-transliteration convention for the PERSIAN source text of Part II (the Persian Hidden Words): a DMG-based scheme with Encyclopaedia-Iranica compatibility. Long vowels by macron (ā ī ū); the Persian consonant digraphs kh (خ), gh (ق/غ), sh (ش), ch (چ), zh (ژ); ʿ for ʿayn and ʾ for hamza; underdots retained on Arabic-origin emphatic/pharyngeal consonants in Arabic loanwords and the embedded Arabic clauses (ṣ ḍ ṭ ẓ ḥ, plus ẕ/ḏ, s/th, q); shadda by doubled consonant; and — crucially — the CLASSICAL ezāfe -i / -yi (pisar-i, sāḥat-i, gulbun-i maʿānī, sabā-yi jānān), NOT the modern spoken -e / -ye, because the vocalized Ocean-of-Lights witness points the classical vowel. The Arabic-embedded clauses and Qur'anic quotations follow the Part I Arabic convention (sun-letter assimilation, hyphenated article).
entries.literal: DMG / Encyclopaedia-Iranica Persian transliteration convention with classical ezāfe
entries.standardEnglish: the Encyclopaedia Iranica / DMG scholarly standard for Persian romanization
entries.wohChoice: the translit field reflects a DMG/Iranica Persian scheme with macron long vowels, kh/gh/sh/ch/zh digraphs, underdots on Arabic-origin consonants, and the classical -i/-yi ezāfe matching the vocalized source; this is a Persian-scoped convention parallel to, and distinct from, the Arabic Part I convention
entries.rationale: Part II is the pipeline's first Persian source text, and the Arabic Part I transliteration entry (dmg-ala-lc-transliteration-convention-hidden-words-woh-arabic) is explicitly Arabic-scoped: it encodes Arabic phonology and Arabic case-vocalization and cannot silently be reused for Persian, which has phonemes (č, ž, g, and the four-way Persian value of the letters that are homographic in Arabic) and an ezāfe construct the Arabic scheme does not cover. This entry ratifies and documents the drafted convention so the translit field is auditable: a DMG-based scheme with Encyclopaedia-Iranica compatibility, the recognised academic standard in Iranian- and Bahá'í-studies scholarship, using macron long vowels and the classical -i/-yi ezāfe because the fully-vocalized Ocean-of-Lights witness points the classical vowel rather than the modern spoken -e/-ye. The retention of underdots on Arabic-origin consonants (and on the numerous embedded Arabic clauses and Qur'anic quotations, which follow the Part I Arabic convention) keeps the loan-stratum and the code-switching into Arabic legible. Named references: the Encyclopaedia Iranica transliteration table (E. Yarshater, ed.); the DMG scheme (Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft); ALA-LC Persian Romanization Tables (Library of Congress). Promotion candidate: to be merged/promoted to central if further Persian Bahá'í / Bábí compositions adopt it.

entries.source: ای X / ای پسر X / ای پسران X / ای فرزند X / ای بنده X / ای بندگان X
entries.translit: ay X / ay pisar-i X / ay pisarān-i X / ay farzand-i X / ay banda-yi X / ay bandagān-i X
entries.lemma: the Persian vocative-address formula that opens every Persian Hidden Word with a shifting ezāfe epithet — the Persian counterpart of the Arabic Part I yā-bna series. Frames: ای X 'O X' (dūst 'Friend'; ghāfilān 'ye heedless'; ʿāṣiyān 'ye transgressors'; muhājirān 'ye emigrants'); ای پسر/پسران X 'O Son/Sons of X'; ای فرزند X 'O child of X'; ای بنده/بندگان X 'O servant(s)'. Epithet inventory (rendered by literal lexical core): rūḥ 'Spirit' (HWP-2,15,38); inṣāf 'Equity' (HWP-4,77); khāk 'Dust' (HWP-5,27,57,68-giyāh, and giyāh-i khāk 'Herb of the Earth'); arḍ 'Earth' (HWP-6,31,64-ẓālimān,63-ahl); ḥubb 'Love' (HWP-7); ʿizz 'Glory' (HWP-8); sāya-yi nābūd 'Fleeting Shadow' (HWP-9); havā 'Passion' (HWP-10,22,79; jawhar-i havā 'Essence of Passion' HWP-28; sāẕij-i havā 'Simpleton of Passion' HWP-50; farzand-i havā HWP-55); turāb 'Dust' (HWP-11,36,62); ṣāḥib-i du chashm 'Possessor of Two Eyes' (HWP-12); jawhar-i ghaflat 'Essence of Heedlessness' (HWP-16); dūst 'Friend' (HWP-3,26,73); jūd 'Bounty' (HWP-29); banda/dunyā 'Servant/Bondslave of the World' (HWP-30,37,40,42,72,81,82; bandagān HWP-80); bīgāna 'the Estranged' (HWP-32); birādar 'Brother' (HWP-33,48,46-ṭarīq); ahl-i riḍvān 'ye that dwell in My Paradise' (HWP-34); ramād 'Ashes' (HWP-39); farzand-i kanīz / pisar-i kanīz 'Son of My Handmaid' (HWP-41,51,58,76,78); rafīq-i ʿarshī 'Companion of the Throne' (HWP-44); maghrūrān bi-amvāl 'ye that pride yourselves on riches' (HWP-53); aghniyā 'Rich Ones' (HWP-54); insān 'Man' (HWP-61); vahm 'Fancy' (HWP-67); ādam 'Adam' (HWP-69); ʿaysh 'Joy' (HWP-70); ghurūr 'Vainglory' (HWP-74); ʿaṣiyān/ẓālimān 'Transgressors/Oppressors' (HWP-64,65); plus the compound vocatives (ṣāḥibān-i hūsh u gūsh 'ye that possess wit and ear' HWP-1; jahalā-yi maʿrūf bi-ʿilm 'ye ignorant renowned for learning' HWP-24; murdagān-i firāsh-i ghaflat 'ye dead upon the couch of heedlessness' HWP-20).
entries.literal: O + [ezāfe epithet]; O Son of / O child of / O servant of + [epithet]
entries.standardEnglish: the authorised Bahá'í World Centre (Shoghi Effendi) translation renders these vocatives with its own fixed epithet-English; it levels the two dust-words (khāk, turāb) both to 'Dust'
entries.wohChoice: rendered literally and epithet-by-epithet by the lexical core, matching the Part I method. The load-bearing sub-decision: Persian khāk and the Arabic loan turāb — both 'dust' — are LEVELLED to 'Dust' as vocatives, because (unlike the Part I insān/bashar pair) they are deployed as interchangeable stylistic synonyms (esp. HWP-48, created min turāb / returning to khāk). The distinct earth-terms gil 'mire/clay' and ramād 'ashes' are kept separate; insān = 'Man' (HWP-61) holds the Part I mapping; bashar does not occur in the Part II vocatives
entries.rationale: The vocative-epithet opening is the structural signature of the Hidden Words in both Parts, and Part II requires its own entry because the Persian construction (ezāfe: ای پسر X) differs morphologically from the Arabic construct (yā bna X) and introduces roughly twenty epithets absent from the Part I inventory (khāk, ramād, ʿaysh, jūd, banda, farzand-i kanīz, sāya-yi nābūd, sāẕij, and the compound vocatives). Each epithet is rendered by its literal lexical core (Dehkhoda, Loghatnāma; Steingass, Persian-English Dictionary; Lane for the Arabic loans), matching the Part I discipline. The one genuinely contestable sub-decision — whether to distinguish khāk from turāb the way Part I distinguished insān from bashar — is resolved the OTHER way, and deliberately: insān and bashar carry distinct lexical emphases (the human as knower vs. the human as mortal flesh), whereas khāk (the ordinary Persian word for dust/soil) and turāb (its Arabic loan-synonym) are used by the author as free stylistic variants — most decisively at HWP-48, where the same sentence has God create all 'from turāb' and return them 'to khāk' in evident parallel. To render them by two different English words would therefore manufacture a distinction the Persian does not mark, violating accuracy-before-lens; both are levelled to 'Dust,' while the genuinely distinct gil 'mire' and ramād 'ashes' remain separate. Marked inferred (not direct) because the epithet-by-epithet literal method and the levelling judgement are defensible scholarly readings rather than the single consensus English. Cross-references: ya-bna-vocative-epithet-series-hidden-words-woh (Arabic Part I); bashar-mortal-quranic-anthropology (central); persian-sufi-bestiary-cosmological-toponyms-hidden-words-woh.

entries.source: بلبل / گل / گلبن / هدهد / سبا / عنقا / قاف / هما / ورقاء
entries.translit: bulbul / gul / gulbun / hudhud / sabā / ʿanqā / qāf / humā / varqāʾ
entries.lemma: the fixed menagerie and cosmological toponyms of the Persian lyric-Sufi register deployed across Part II: bulbul 'nightingale', gul / gulbun / gulshan 'rose / rose-bower / rose-garden', ṭayr / ṭuyūr 'bird(s)', varqāʾ 'dove' (Arabic; HWP-13), hudhud 'hoopoe' (the Solomon-and-Sheba bird of Qur'an 27; HWP-1), ʿanqā 'the mythic bird = phoenix', the analogue of the Sīmurgh, dweller upon Qāf (HWP-1), qāf 'the world-encircling cosmic mountain' (HWP-1), humā 'the fortune-/crown-bestowing bird of Persian lore' (HWP-38), sabā 'Sheba' (the queendom of the hoopoe's errand, HWP-1)
entries.partOfSpeech: Persian Sufi-lyric technical imagery: bestiary + cosmological toponyms
entries.literal: nightingale / rose(-bower) / bird / dove / hoopoe / phoenix / Mount Qáf / Humá-bird / Sheba
entries.standardEnglish: English renderings vary between glossing the images and transliterating the named entities; the mythic bird ʿanqā/Sīmurgh is variously 'phoenix', 'griffin', or left transliterated
entries.wohChoice: a hybrid retain-vs-gloss policy: the common lyric images are rendered by English gloss (bulbul = 'nightingale'; gul/gulbun/gulshan = 'rose'/'rose-bower'/'rose-garden'; varqāʾ = 'dove'; ṭayr = 'bird'; hudhud = 'hoopoe'), while the named cosmological/mythic entities that have no clean English equivalent are RETAINED as proper names: Qáf (the cosmic mountain), Humá (kept as 'the Humá-bird', distinct from the phoenix). ʿanqā is rendered 'phoenix' (its nearest analogue) but kept lexically distinct from Humá; sabā is rendered by the biblical/Qur'anic proper name 'Sheba'
entries.rationale: Part II is saturated with the technical imagery of the Persian mystical lyric — the nightingale and rose, the hoopoe of Solomon, the ʿanqā upon Mount Qáf, the Humá — each carrying a settled valence in the tradition of ʿAṭṭār's Manṭiq al-ṭayr (The Conference of the Birds) and the ghazals of Ḥāfiẓ, where the birds are stations of the soul and Qáf the goal of the mystic quest. A blanket policy in either direction fails: transliterating the common images (bulbul, gul) would estrange a reader for no gain, while glossing the named cosmological entities (Qáf as 'the mountain', Humá as 'a bird of fortune') would erase proper names that function as fixed loci in the cosmology and have no English equivalent. The WoH translation therefore glosses the common metaphors and retains the named entities, rendering ʿanqā by its nearest English analogue 'phoenix' (the ʿanqā mughrib being the Arabic-Persian counterpart of the self-renewing bird) while keeping it distinct from Humá, which is left as a proper name because the crown-conferring Humá of Persian lore has no English match. sabā is the proper name 'Sheba' (Qur'an 27:22-44; 1 Kings 10). Marked inferred because the retain-vs-gloss line and the ʿanqā=phoenix / Sīmurgh identification are defensible scholarly choices, not the only possible ones (a maximalist could retain ʿAnqá and Sīmurgh transliterated). Named references: F. al-Dīn ʿAṭṭār, Manṭiq al-ṭayr; A. Schimmel, Mystical Dimensions of Islam (UNC 1975); the entries 'ʿAnqāʾ', 'Sīmorḡ', 'Qāf' in the Encyclopaedia Iranica. Cross-reference: persian-vocative-epithet-series-hidden-words-woh.

entries.source: جبل فاران / اصحاب مدين / بقعه مبارکه زمان
entries.translit: jabal-i Fārān / aṣḥāb-i Madyan / buqʿa-yi mubāraka-yi zamān
entries.lemma: the Sinai-covenant geography of HWP-71, where Bahá'u'lláh sites the primordial covenant: jabal-i Fārān = Mount Fārān/Paran (the Sinai-region peak of Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3); aṣḥāb-i Madyan = 'the companions of Midian' (the region of Moses's exile and covenant with Jethro, Exodus 2-3); and buqʿa-yi mubāraka-yi zamān = 'the blessed precinct of zamān', where buqʿa mubāraka is the Qur'anic Sinai phrase (al-buqʿa al-mubāraka, Qur'an 28:30) and zamān is the crux term — common noun 'time' vs. a putative place-name
entries.partOfSpeech: Persian/Arabic proper toponyms + one contested common-noun/toponym crux
entries.literal: Mount Paran / the companions of Midian / the blessed precinct of time
entries.standardEnglish: the authorised Bahá'í World Centre (Shoghi Effendi) translation renders zamān as a named locus ('the hallowed precincts of Zamán')
entries.wohChoice: Fārān = 'Mount Párán' (Paran); Madyan = 'Midian'; and zamān rendered as the common noun 'Time' ('the blessed precinct of Time') rather than as a named locus 'Zamán' — an English edit from the draft's provisional 'the blessed precincts of Zamán'
entries.rationale: HWP-71 sites the pre-eternal covenant in Mosaic-Sinai geography, and two of the three toponyms are secure proper names rendered by their biblical/Qur'anic forms: Fārān is Paran, the peak named beside Sinai and Seir in the theophany of Deuteronomy 33:2 and Habakkuk 3:3, and Madyan is Midian, the region of Moses's exile (Exodus 2-3; Qur'an 28:22-28). The crux is zamān. The surrounding phrase buqʿa mubāraka is itself lifted from the Qur'anic Sinai theophany (al-buqʿa al-mubāraka, 'the blessed spot', Qur'an 28:30), which sets a geographic expectation; but no Sinai toponym 'Zamān' is attested anywhere, and the plain lexical value of زمان is the common noun 'time'. Accuracy-before-lens therefore prefers 'the blessed precinct of Time', reading the site of the primordial covenant as a metaphysical rather than a cartographic locus — coherent with the pre-eternal Covenant of alastu bi-rabbikum ('Am I not your Lord?', Qur'an 7:172), the Day of the Covenant to which the aphorism appeals — and this reading also keeps the WoH text independent of the authorised translation, which reifies zamān into a place-name. Marked inferred because both readings are defensible and the named-locus alternative is recorded, not dismissed; the decision turns on the absence of any attested toponym plus the plain-sense priority. These toponyms are the natural site of comparative-tradition (Sinai/covenant) commentary, which is the Editor's to write in the apparatus, not the Translator's to build into the line. Named references: BDB and HALOT s.v. פארן (Paran) and מדין (Midian); the Sinai-theophany cluster Deuteronomy 33:2 / Habakkuk 3:3 / Qur'an 28:30.
